metadata.title: Filtering and Finishing Maple Syrup
metadata.description: After the evaporation process has removed much of the water from the concentrated sap, diatomaceous earth is then added which acts as a final filter aid. Once the sap is brought to a sugar content of at least 66 percent sugar at 68 degrees Fahrenheit, it can legally be labeled as syrup in New York. Vermont and New Hampshire require a minimum sugar percent of 66.9. By taking readings with both a thermometer and a hydrometer, the syrup can be 'drawn off' when it hits the correct sugar percent at the correct temperature.

summary.brief: A man adds diatomaceous earth to hot maple syrup, filters it into a barrel, measures its density and temperature, calculates the sugar content, and the video ends with credit slides.
summary.detailed: The clip opens with a black title screen that reads “Filtering and Finishing Maple Syrup.” A man wearing a green‑and‑white checked shirt appears, adds two cups of diatomaceous earth to about five gallons of hot maple syrup, and stirs the mixture with a scoop. He then activates a pump that forces the syrup through a canister filter into a metal barrel, where a faint red “hot‑test” line is visible as the syrup fills the barrel. Just before the barrel is full, he drops a hydrometer into the syrup, noting a reading of roughly 60.5, and inserts a temperature probe that reads 187‑188 °F. Using a chart, he determines the sugar concentration to be about 66.5 %, meeting the legal minimum for maple syrup. Bottles of syrup are visible on a shelf in the background. The segment concludes with a series of slides: a USDA National Agroforestry Center title, acknowledgments of Virginia Tech and Cornell University, and a final screen inviting viewers to visit the extension website.

summary_sent_to_llm.title: Filtering and Finishing Maple Syrup
summary_sent_to_llm.description: After the evaporation process has removed much of the water from the concentrated sap, diatomaceous earth is then added which acts as a final filter aid. Once the sap is brought to a sugar content of at least 66 percent sugar at 68 degrees Fahrenheit, it can legally be labeled as syrup in New York. Vermont and New Hampshire require a minimum sugar percent of 66.9. By taking readings with both a thermometer and a hydrometer, the syrup can be 'drawn off' when it hits the correct sugar percent at the correct temperature.
summary_sent_to_llm.root_summary: The clip opens with a black title screen that reads “Filtering and Finishing Maple Syrup.” A man wearing a green‑and‑white checked shirt appears, adds two cups of diatomaceous earth to about five gallons of hot maple syrup, and stirs the mixture with a scoop. He then activates a pump that forces the syrup through a canister filter into a metal barrel, where a faint red “hot‑test” line is visible as the syrup fills the barrel. Just before the barrel is full, he drops a hydrometer into the syrup, noting a reading of roughly 60.5, and inserts a temperature probe that reads 187‑188 °F. Using a chart, he determines the sugar concentration to be about 66.5 %, meeting the legal minimum for maple syrup. Bottles of syrup are visible on a shelf in the background. The segment concludes with a series of slides: a USDA National Agroforestry Center title, acknowledgments of Virginia Tech and Cornell University, and a final screen inviting viewers to visit the extension website.
